newsitem.title: USA: once on, tough to get off.
newsitem.headline: once on, tough to get off.

text.p: Getting off the U.S. black list of alleged state sponsors of terrorism is extremely tough even when Washington concedes it can no longer trace a direct link to terror attacks, the State Department's latest report on such violence made clear on Wednesday.

Since the first congressionally mandated annual list appeared in 1979, Iraq is the only country that was formally removed, in 1982, requiring a presidential determination. It was restored a month after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
South Yemen was dropped from the list when it merged with North Yemen in 1990 and ceased to exist.

Now, for the third year running, the secretary of state has branded an unchanged list of seven nations, five of them in the Middle East, as "state sponsors of terrorism": Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Libya, North Korea, Sudan and Syria.

The State Department acknowleded that several of the alleged culprits were not directly involved last year in international "terrorism," which it defined as "pre-meditated, politically motivated violence perpetrated against noncombatant targets by subnational groups or clandestine agents, usually intended to influence an audience."
Cuba, for instance, "no longer actively supports armed struggle in Latin America and other parts of the world," said the report, "Patterns of Global Terrorism, 1996."

But it said: "Although there is no current evidence that Cuban officials were directly involved in sponsoring specific acts of terrorism last year, Cuba is still a safe haven for several international terrorists, maintains close relations with other state sponsors of terrorism, and remains in contact with numerous leftist insurgent groups in Latin America."

Likewise, North Korea, the other non-Middle Eastern alleged state sponsor of terrorism, "cannot be conclusively linked to any international terrorist attacks since 1987," the department said. It said the isolated, heavily armed Stalinist state continued to provide sanctuary to members of the Japanese Red Army but it added the Red Army was no longer active in Japan as a terrorist group.
The department also cleared Sudan and Syria of any direct role in international terrorism, defined as "involving citizens or the territory of more than one country."

It said Sudan last year "took some positive steps to distance itself from its past support for terrorism," though it allegedly continued to serve as a "sanctuary and training centre for for several international terrorist groups" including the radical Palestinian group Hamas and the Iranian-inspired Hizballah, or Party of God.

Syria, which complained loudly about being included on the list despite its participation in the stalled U.S.-brokered Middle East peace process, was cleared of active involvement for the past 10 years but tarred for continuing to harbour guerrilla groups.

"The United States continues to urge Syria to banish terrorist groups that maintain a presence in Syrian-controlled territory in Lebanon," the report said. "Until Syria does so, it will remain on the list of state sponsors."
The department said Iran remained the chief state sponsor of terrorism, "involved in the planning and execution of terrorist acts by its own agents and others ..."

Iraq, the only country to have been removed from the black list and then restored, "has not managed to recover its pre-Gulf war international terrorist capabilities," the report said. But it said Iraq was "slowly rebuilding its intelligence network" and continued to provide safe haven to Palestinian groups opposed to any negotiated peace with Israel.

Alleged Libyan terror has been sharply reduced by United Nations sanctions following the November 1991 indictments of two Libyan nationals for the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988, the report said.
